photometry.formula: mag = mag_sun - 2.5*log10(I_sc/I_sun); I_sc/I_sun = (1/d^2) * (2/3) * (C_d/pi^2) * r^2 * (sin(a) + (pi - a)*cos(a)); d = observer-object distance (same units as r), r = sphere radius, a = solar phase angle (rad, Sun-object-observer), C_d = Lambertian diffuse reflection coefficient. Equivalent area form (Wilmer 2022): Mv = mag_sun - 2.5*log10(A*Psi/d^2), Psi = (2/3)*(C_d/pi)*(sin(a)+(pi-a)*cos(a)), A = cross-section area.
photometry.albedo_default_note: Chow et al. 2021 (diffuse sphere, 1 m^2 cross-section, reflectance 0.2) and Gorman et al. 2023 (1.5 m diameter, albedo 0.2). Alternatives in literature: 0.17 (Bolden 2020), 0.5 (Bhadauria 2024), 0.86 (Wilmer 2022).

placement_findings.finding: Single P/3 lunar-resonant or chaotic-orbit observer reached 27% of a 475,000 km 4pi domain; all other single-orbit types <10%. Adding satellites in one orbit type increases revisits but not coverage; mixing orbit types is required.

GEO + Lagrange + chaotic constellation with 42 cm optics gave persistent custody of a waxing-crescent free-return trajectory except for the hardest 1.5 days; a 75-satellite LEO constellation is blind in the sunward hemisphere.

Moon-centered volume: 99.9% coverage with 5 satellites at 0.3 m; 100% with 9 satellites at 0.5 m; >90% with 3 sats at 0.3 m or 13 sats at 0.1 m. Earth-Moon corridor needs 0.6-0.8 m apertures and >=7 satellites for >90% (or 15+ at 0.3-0.5 m).
12 observers in an L1 halo saw an NRHO target 99.28% of 30 days (L2 halo 98.96%); touring periodic orbits slightly worse for NRHO surveillance.

With 10 optimally placed observers, custody of objects maneuvering off L2 Lyapunov/halo or NRHO orbits is nearly guaranteed at limiting magnitude 18 with Sun 30/Moon 10/Earth 15 deg exclusions; one observer cannot guarantee custody.

Single libration-orbit observer coverage of the cone of shame degrades below cutoff mag 18 and is 0% at mag <=16; at mag 16, 2 observers reach ~44% and 4 reach 63%; at mag 17, 2 observers reach ~95%. Orbit-family diversity and small phase offsets help.

For demand across L1 and L2, a large 1:1 resonant L1 Lyapunov is advantageous; observers on 1:1 resonant orbits cluster leading/trailing because solar phase dominates; for L2-centered demand, 2:1 and 3:1 resonant L2 halos are favored.

Earth-Moon 2:1 resonant orbits precess to cover the whole cislunar disc in ~20 revolutions (~26-day period), have benign uncertainty growth, and are trackable by a global magnitude-20 ground network; a lunar-surface sensor adds little for these orbits.

L2 halo targets are hard to observe from all observer families; L4 planar orbits perform well both as observers and as targets; Moon orbits are dramatically better than Earth orbits for observing L1/L2 objects.
Global ground optical network simulation of Artemis I left ~9 continuous days unobservable; most sensors saw <20% of the trajectory.

No ground-based sensor can fully avoid solar exclusion; spaceborne tandem observers offset from the Earth-Sun line can largely avoid it; collinear Lagrange points have the most significant exclusion periods.
